I N T E G R A T I N G S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y I N T O B U S I N E S S F U N C T I O N S
Sustainable Marketing
& Branding
Developing and communicating sustainable products and services — without overclaiming
01

B E F O R E W E B E G I N
Since 27 September 2026, calling a product “eco-friendly” 
without proof is illegal across the EU.
India’s regulator issued equivalent guidelines in October 2024.
Marketing used to be the one function allowed to describe sustainability in adjectives. Today it has to describe it in 
evidence — and that changes how products are designed, priced, and sold.
SUSTAINABLE MARKETING & BRANDING 02

B Y T H E E N D O F T H I S L E C T U R E
You will be able to…
Design
Apply the green marketing mix —
product, price, place, promotion — to a 
sustainable offering.
Calculate
Frame a sustainable product’s price 
premium as lifetime cost and avoided 
emissions.
Evaluate
Test any environmental claim against five 
principles and current Indian and EU 
rules.
Connect
Explain what marketing needs from 
every other business function to keep its 
promises.
SUSTAINABLE MARKETING & BRANDING 03

T O D A Y ’ S J O U R N E Y
Marketing: The Function That Speaks for All the Others
Sustainability is integrated function by function. Marketing sits at the customer interface — so it is both the loudest voice and the most exposed to legal and 
reputational risk.
01
Developing Sustainable 
Offerings
What makes an offering genuinely more 
sustainable — and how to price and 
position it.
02
Communicating Credibly
Claims, labels, and storytelling that 
customers and regulators can both trust.
03
Greenwashing & 
Regulation
The seven sins, and the rules now in 
force in India, the EU, the UK, and the 
US.
04
Purpose-Driven Branding
Turning proof into brand value — and 
what Patagonia and H&M teach us.
SUSTAINABLE MARKETING & BRANDING 04

S E C T I O N 1 O F 4
Developing Sustainable Offerings
Marketing starts before the campaign: with what is actually being sold.
05

S E C T I O N 1 · T H E F R A M E W O R K
The Green Marketing Mix: The Four Ps, Reimagined
The classic marketing mix still applies — but each P carries a sustainability decision.
Product
Design for lower impact and longer life; 
substantiate improvements with LCA 
data rather than adjectives.
Price
Price on lifetime cost, not sticker price; 
decide deliberately whether to charge a 
premium, match, or move to a service 
model.
Place
Low-carbon distribution and availability 
where customers already shop, plus refill 
or take-back points that make the 
sustainable choice convenient.
Promotion
Honest, specific communication that 
helps customers choose and use the 
product well — the subject of Sections 2 
and 3.
SUSTAINABLE MARKETING & BRANDING 06

S E C T I O N 1 · P R O D U C T D E S I G N
Design Decisions Lock In the Impact
The LCA lecture showed where impacts sit; design is where they are decided — long before any advertisement is written.
Design for Durability & Repair A longer life spreads the embedded impact of making the product over more years of use — often the single 
biggest lever.
Design for Disassembly & Recycling Mono-materials, removable batteries, and labelled components keep materials in the technical cycle instead of 
the landfill.
Design for Efficient Use Where the use phase dominates (appliances, vehicles), energy and water in use matter far more than packaging 
— Scope 3 Category 11.
Design for Less Material Lightweighting, concentrates, and refills cut material and transport impact per use — and are easy to explain 
honestly.
SUSTAINABLE MARKETING & BRANDING 07

S E C T I O N 1 · U N D E R S T A N D I N G T H E C U S T O M E R
The Attitude–Behaviour Gap
Why “customers say they care” does not automatically become “customers buy it”.
The Gap Surveys routinely find far more people intend to buy sustainable products than actually do — researchers call 
this the attitude–behaviour (or intention–action) gap (Carrington, Neville & Whitwell, 2010).
Why It Happens Price premiums, limited availability, doubt about whether claims are true, habit, convenience, and unclear 
personal benefit all stand between intention and purchase.
What It Means for Marketers Do not rely on values alone. Make the sustainable option the affordable, convenient, default, and verifiable one 
— and show the personal payoff.
SUSTAINABLE MARKETING & BRANDING 08

S E C T I O N 1 · W O R K E D E X A M P L E
Selling on Lifetime Cost: A 5-Star vs. 3-Star Appliance
G I V E N
Product A (3-star): ₹40,000; uses 1,200 kWh per year
Product B (5-star): ₹48,000; uses 800 kWh per year
Tariff ₹8/kWh; 10-year life; grid factor 0.727 kgCO₂e/kWh (illustrative)
F O R M U L A
Lifetime Cost = Purchase Price + (Annual kWh × Tariff × Years)
S T E P - BY - S T E P C A L C U L A T I O N
1 Product A: ₹40,000 + (1,200 × ₹8 × 10) = ₹40,000 + ₹96,000 = ₹1,36,000
2 Product B: ₹48,000 + (800 × ₹8 × 10) = ₹48,000 + ₹64,000 = ₹1,12,000
3 Saving with B: ₹1,36,000 − ₹1,12,000 = ₹24,000; the ₹8,000 premium is repaid in 8,000 ÷ 3,200 = 2.5 years
4 Emissions avoided: 400 kWh × 0.727 kgCO₂e × 10 years ≈ 2,908 kg ≈ 2.9 tCO₂e
₹24,000 + 2.9 t CO₂e
Reframing the sticker-price premium as a lifetime saving is both the most honest and the most persuasive message. (Figures are 
illustrative, not product data.)
SUSTAINABLE MARKETING & BRANDING 09

S E C T I O N 1 · B U S I N E S S M O D E L S
Beyond the Product: Selling the Service
Some of the strongest sustainability offers change what is sold, not just how it is made.
Repair & Maintenance
Lifetime repair services extend product 
life and deepen loyalty — Patagonia’s 
repair and Worn Wear programmes are 
the best-known example.
Refill & Reuse
Refillable packaging and deposit-return 
systems remove single-use material 
entirely, if convenience keeps pace.
Resale & Take-Back
Buying back used products for 
refurbishment or resale keeps value and 
materials circulating — the circular 
economy at the till.
Leasing & Subscription
Selling use instead of ownership aligns 
the seller’s profit with durability, because 
the seller keeps the asset.
SUSTAINABLE MARKETING & BRANDING 10

◆ INTERACTIVE C H E C K Y O U R U N D E R S T A N D I N G
Why is it usually more persuasive to market a 5-star appliance on 
lifetime cost than on its sticker price?
A Sticker prices are not allowed in sustainability advertising
B
The upfront premium is repaid through savings, so lifetime cost reframes the premium as 
a saving
C Lifetime cost hides the real price from the customer
D Star labels only matter for exported products
A N S W E R & W H Y
B. The upfront premium is repaid through 
savings, so lifetime cost reframes the 
premium as a saving
In the worked example the ₹8,000 premium is repaid 
in 2.5 years and saves ₹24,000 over ten years. 
Showing that is honest, verifiable, and speaks to the 
customer’s own interest — the attitude–behaviour 
gap’s biggest barrier is price.
SUSTAINABLE MARKETING & BRANDING 11

S E C T I O N 2 O F 4
Communicating Credibly
A claim is only as strong as the evidence a sceptical stranger could check.
12

S E C T I O N 2 · T H E S T A N D A R D
Five Principles of a Credible Claim
Distilled from regulator guidance in India, the EU, and the UK — a checklist to run before anything is published.
Specific
Say exactly what and how 
much — “60% recycled 
content” — not “eco” or 
“green”.
Substantiated
Keep an evidence file behind 
every claim; use independent 
verification wherever possible.
Relevant
Talk about impacts that 
matter, not legal baselines or 
trivial attributes.
Complete
Consider the full life cycle and 
disclose important trade-offs 
rather than hiding them.
Proportionate
Claim no more than the 
evidence supports — including 
comparisons and future 
targets.
SUSTAINABLE MARKETING & BRANDING 13

S E C T I O N 2 · I N P R A C T I C E
Vague vs. Verifiable: Rewriting the Same Message
At-Risk Claim Credible Version
“Our bottle is eco-friendly.” Made from 60% recycled PET, verified by an independent auditor; the other 
40% is virgin resin.
“Carbon-neutral shipping.” We cut delivery emissions per parcel by 18% since 2023 (third-party verified); 
removal projects are funded separately and reported separately.
“Good for the planet.” Uses 30% less electricity than the 3-star equivalent, per the BEE energy label.
“Net zero soon.” Targets validated by the Science Based Targets initiative, with interim 
milestones and annual progress reporting.
SUSTAINABLE MARKETING & BRANDING 14

S E C T I O N 2 · T H E L A B E L L A N D S C A P E
Ecolabels: Three Types, Three Levels of Trust
The ISO 14020 family classifies environmental labels by who checks the claim.
Type I · ISO 14024
Third-party programmes with published 
criteria and independent verification —
for example the EU Ecolabel or 
Germany’s Blue Angel.
Type II · ISO 14021
Self-declared claims by the 
manufacturer. Legitimate, but only if 
specific, verifiable, and not misleading.
Type III · ISO 14025
Environmental Product Declarations: 
LCA-based, quantified, third-party 
verified — data, not a pass/fail badge.
India: BEE & Ecomark
BEE Star Labels rate appliance energy 
efficiency; Ecomark is India’s ecolabelling 
scheme for products.
SUSTAINABLE MARKETING & BRANDING 15

◆ INTERACTIVE C L A S S I F Y T H E C L A I M
Credible or At Risk?
For each claim, decide whether it is credible as written or at risk under current guidance.
1 “Eco-friendly” printed on packaging, with no explanation
2 “Contains 60% post-consumer recycled plastic,” audited by a third party
3 “Carbon-neutral product,” achieved purely through carbon offsets
4 “25% lower cradle-to-gate CO₂e than our 2023 model,” per a reviewed LCA
5 Green leaf imagery and “good for the planet” on a plastic-heavy product
6 “Uses 30% less electricity than the 3-star equivalent,” per BEE label data
CREDIBLE AT RISK
2 1
4 3
6 5
SUSTAINABLE MARKETING & BRANDING 16

◆ INTERACTIVE C H E C K Y O U R U N D E R S T A N D I N G
Which type of ecolabel is an Environmental Product Declaration (EPD)?
A Type I (ISO 14024) — third-party ecolabel programme
B Type II (ISO 14021) — self-declared claim
C Type III (ISO 14025) — quantified, LCA-based, third-party verified declaration
D None of the ISO ecolabel types
A N S W E R & W H Y
C. Type III (ISO 14025) — quantified, LCA￾based, third-party verified declaration
EPDs are Type III declarations: they report quantified 
life cycle data (from an LCA, as in our previous lecture) 
and are third-party verified, but they do not rank a 
product as good or bad.
SUSTAINABLE MARKETING & BRANDING 17

S E C T I O N 3 O F 4
Greenwashing & Regulation
The line between persuasion and deception is now written into law.
18

S E C T I O N 3 · T H E T A X O N O M Y
The Seven Sins of Greenwashing (TerraChoice, 2007)
Hidden Trade-off
Green on one attribute while ignoring larger 
impacts elsewhere.
No Proof
A claim with no accessible evidence or 
credible certification.
Vagueness
Poorly defined terms such as “all-natural” or 
“eco”.
Irrelevance
True but unimportant — or already required 
by law.
Lesser of Two Evils
Green within a category that is harmful 
overall.
Fibbing
Claims that are simply false.
Worshipping False Labels
Fake seals or implied endorsements that do 
not exist.
SUSTAINABLE MARKETING & BRANDING 19

S E C T I O N 3 · T H E R U L E S
Four Jurisdictions, One Direction of Travel
Different tools, same message: claims must be specific, evidenced, and not misleading.
India
CCPA Greenwashing Guidelines (15 Oct 
2024): generic terms need qualifiers and 
substantiation; aspirational claims need 
an actionable plan.
European Union
Directive (EU) 2024/825, applying from 
27 Sep 2026: bans generic claims without 
proof, offset-based neutrality claims, and 
self-made labels.
United Kingdom
CMA Green Claims Code (2021); in 2022 
the CMA opened a fashion-sector 
investigation covering ASOS, Boohoo, 
and others.
United States
FTC Green Guides (last revised 2012): 
guidance rather than statute, enforced 
through deceptive-advertising law, state 
actions, and class suits.
SUSTAINABLE MARKETING & BRANDING 20

S E C T I O N 3 · I N D I A
India’s CCPA Greenwashing Guidelines, 2024
Issued by the Central Consumer Protection Authority on 15 October 2024, complementing the 2022 misleading-advertisements guidelines.
Who Is Covered Manufacturers, service providers, traders, advertising agencies, and endorsers — every party that makes or 
amplifies an environmental claim.
Generic Terms Need Backing Words such as “green”, “eco-friendly”, “sustainable”, “natural”, “pure” or “carbon-neutral” cannot be used 
without adequate, accurate, accessible qualifiers and substantiation.
The Evidence Standard Claims need verifiable evidence — independent third-party certification is accepted — and comparative claims 
must rest on relevant data disclosed to consumers.
Aspirational Claims Future-facing claims such as “net zero by 2050” are acceptable only when clear, actionable plans exist to deliver 
them.
SUSTAINABLE MARKETING & BRANDING 21

S E C T I O N 3 · E U R O P E A N U N I O N
The EU’s Green Claims Rules: Timeline
27 Mar 2024
Directive (EU) 2024/825 enters into force, 
amending EU consumer-protection law.
27 Mar 2026
Deadline for Member States to write the 
directive into national law.
27 Sep 2026
Rules apply to traders, with no transition 
period for products already on the market.
After Sep 2026
National authorities and courts enforce; the 
separate Green Claims Directive proposal has 
been paused since 2025.
SUSTAINABLE MARKETING & BRANDING 22

S E C T I O N 3 · E U R O P E A N U N I O N
What the EU Now Prohibits
The directive amends the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive — these practices are now unfair by definition.
Generic Environmental Claims “Eco-friendly”, “green”, “climate-friendly” and similar are banned unless the trader can show recognised 
excellent environmental performance relevant to the claim.
Offset-Based Neutrality Claims Saying a product is climate neutral, or has a reduced or positive impact, because of greenhouse-gas offsetting is 
prohibited at product level.
Self-Made Sustainability Labels Labels must rest on a certification scheme or be established by public authorities; a company’s own badge no 
longer counts.
Unsupported Future Claims Claims about future performance need a detailed, time-bound implementation plan, verified by an independent 
expert, with the findings made available.
SUSTAINABLE MARKETING & BRANDING 23

◆ INTERACTIVE C A S E S T U D Y
When a “Conscious” Label Meets a Regulator: H&M
H&M’s “Conscious Choice” collection and Higg Index scorecards (2019–2022)
Regulators in the Netherlands and Norway challenged H&M’s use of labels such as “Conscious” and of Higg Materials Sustainability Index scores, arguing that the claims 
were unclear and insufficiently substantiated.
The Regulatory Response
Norway’s Consumer Authority criticised the Conscious collection in 2019 and warned in 
June 2022 that Higg-based marketing could be misleading; the Dutch ACM found unclear, 
insufficiently substantiated claims.
The Outcome
In September 2022 H&M removed “Conscious Choice” indicators from its online shops 
worldwide, dropped a “more sustainable materials” heading, and donated €500,000 to 
sustainability organisations.
The Industry Ripple
The Sustainable Apparel Coalition paused its consumer-facing Higg transparency 
programme on 27 June 2022, and the UK CMA opened its fashion-sector probe in July 
2022.
The Balance
H&M said the concerns did not involve “false information”, and US class actions have had 
mixed outcomes: the lesson is about clarity and substantiation, not a finding of fraud.
SUSTAINABLE MARKETING & BRANDING 24

S E C T I O N 3 · T H E O P P O S I T E R I S K
Greenhushing: When Fear Silences Real Progress
Regulation punishes overclaiming — but staying silent has its own cost.
What It Is Companies deliberately under-communicate real sustainability progress to avoid scrutiny or backlash —
“greenhushing”.
Why It Is a Problem Customers, investors, and suppliers cannot reward progress they never hear about, and best practice does not 
spread.
The Remedy: Say Less, Prove More Communicate specific, modest, evidenced progress — including what is not yet solved. Precision is protection 
against both greenwashing and greenhushing.
SUSTAINABLE MARKETING & BRANDING 25

◆ INTERACTIVE T H I N K & S H A R E
“Your product’s emissions per unit fell 18%, but total 
company emissions rose because sales grew. What can 
you truthfully say in an advertisement?”
Think about intensity versus absolute claims — and what a regulator would ask you to prove.
3 MIN
SUSTAINABLE MARKETING & BRANDING 26

◆ INTERACTIVE C H E C K Y O U R U N D E R S T A N D I N G
From 27 September 2026, which claim is banned as an unfair practice 
across the EU?
A “Contains 60% recycled material,” verified by an independent auditor
B A product-level “carbon neutral” claim based on greenhouse-gas offsetting
C Publishing an LCA-based Environmental Product Declaration
D Any mention of sustainability in advertising
A N S W E R & W H Y
B. A product-level “carbon neutral” claim 
based on greenhouse-gas offsetting
Directive (EU) 2024/825 prohibits product-level 
climate-neutral claims that rest on offsetting. Specific, 
verified claims and EPDs remain allowed — which links 
directly back to our carbon-markets lecture on offset 
quality.
SUSTAINABLE MARKETING & BRANDING 27

S E C T I O N 4 O F 4
Purpose-Driven Branding
Trust is the asset: earned by deeds first, and only then by messages.
28

S E C T I O N 4 · B R A N D P U R P O S E
Three Tests for Purpose-Driven Branding
Purpose is not a slogan; it is a promise the whole company has to be able to keep.
Authentic The commitment connects to the company’s core business — not to a side campaign that leaves the main 
product line untouched.
Material It addresses the impacts that actually dominate the footprint (the hotspots found by LCA and Scope 3 analysis), 
not just the easy ones.
Verifiable Progress is measured, published, and open to scrutiny — including setbacks. The say–do gap destroys trust 
faster than it was built.
SUSTAINABLE MARKETING & BRANDING 29

◆ INTERACTIVE C A S E S T U D Y
When an Ad Told Customers Not to Buy: Patagonia
“Don’t Buy This Jacket” — Black Friday, 25 November 2011
Patagonia ran a full-page New York Times ad for its best-selling R2 fleece, listing the jacket’s real environmental costs and directing readers to its Common Threads 
Initiative — repair, reuse, resale, recycling.
Why It Was Credible
It rested on real prior action: repair services, take-back, used-gear resale (later Worn 
Wear), and unusual openness about the impacts of its own products.
The Reported Result
Sales rose roughly 30% in the months that followed, as widely reported; the exact window 
and causation vary by source.
The Honest Reading
The ad built trust and preference; it did not obviously reduce total consumption. Imitators 
without Patagonia’s track record risk a backlash.
The Lesson
Credibility is earned by deeds first. The ad worked because the company had already 
earned the right to say it.
SUSTAINABLE MARKETING & BRANDING 30

S E C T I O N 4 · B E Y O N D T H E C O N S U M E R
B2B, Employer, and Investor Audiences
Sustainable branding is not only aimed at shoppers — your most demanding audiences read the evidence closely.
Business Customers Large buyers now ask suppliers for product carbon footprints and EPDs — recall Walmart’s Project Gigaton 
reaching 5,000+ suppliers. Verified data is sales collateral.
Employer Brand Sustainability performance influences recruitment and retention, especially among graduates — the audience in 
this room.
Investors and Regulators Marketing claims and disclosures such as BRSR are read side by side; inconsistency between them is itself a red 
flag.
SUSTAINABLE MARKETING & BRANDING 31

S E C T I O N 4 · M E A S U R E M E N T
How to Tell Whether Sustainable Marketing Is Working
Both commercial results and integrity need KPIs — and both should be reported.
Revenue Share
Share of revenue from offerings meeting 
a published sustainability definition —
define the criteria first.
Claim Coverage
Percentage of public claims with an 
evidence file and legal review before 
publication.
Trust & Complaints
Brand-trust scores, greenwashing 
complaints, and regulator queries — the 
early-warning indicators.
Behaviour Outcomes
Repeat purchase, repair and take-back 
uptake, and refill rates — proof 
customers actually acted.
SUSTAINABLE MARKETING & BRANDING 32

◆ INTERACTIVE C H E C K Y O U R U N D E R S T A N D I N G
What made Patagonia’s “Don’t Buy This Jacket” credible rather than 
cynical?
A It was the cheapest ad it could buy
B It was backed by years of repair, reuse, and transparency actions
C It guaranteed that sales would fall
D It avoided mentioning the jacket’s environmental impact
A N S W E R & W H Y
B. It was backed by years of repair, reuse, 
and transparency actions
The ad’s credibility came from prior action — repair 
services, resale, and honest impact disclosure. 
Without that track record, the same message would 
look like greenwashing with a twist.
SUSTAINABLE MARKETING & BRANDING 33

B R I N G I N G I T T O G E T H E R
Marketing Can Only Promise What Other Functions Deliver
Integrating sustainability into business functions means each function supplies the proof that marketing then communicates.
R&D / Design LCA-informed product improvements that make real, specific claims possible.
Procurement Certified inputs and supplier data (Scope 3 Category 1) to back sourcing claims.
Operations & Logistics Measured energy, waste, and transport performance, including mode-shift gains.
Finance Investment for greener products, and numbers that match what is disclosed (for example BRSR).
Legal & Compliance Claim review against CCPA- and EU-style rules before anything is published.
IT & Data Traceability and data systems so every claim can be evidenced on demand.
SUSTAINABLE MARKETING & BRANDING 34

B R I N G I N G I T T O G E T H E R
The Sustainable Marketing Loop
Four steps, repeated: each one is only credible if the previous one is real.
1. Develop Design offerings with measurably lower impact, guided by LCA and customer insight.
2. Substantiate Build the evidence file: data, certifications, EPDs, and legal review.
3. Communicate Apply the five principles: specific, substantiated, relevant, complete, proportionate.
4. Verify & Improve Track KPIs and complaints, correct mistakes openly, and feed lessons back into design.
SUSTAINABLE MARKETING & BRANDING 35

◆ INTERACTIVE A P P L Y I T A L L
“Pick an advertisement you have seen recently. Which of 
the five principles does it meet — and which would a 
regulator challenge first?”
This is exactly how a claims-review meeting begins in practice.
4 MIN
SUSTAINABLE MARKETING & BRANDING 36

B . T E C H F I N A L Y E A R · C O M P U T E R S C I E N C E & E N G I N E E R I N G · O P E N E L E C T I V E
I N T E G R A T I N G S U S T A I N A B I L I T Y I N T O B U S I N E S S F U N C T I O N S
Sustainable
Finance
Accessing green finance and integrating ESG factors into financial decision-making
C O U R S E
Sustainability & Climate Change
K E Y F R A M E W O R K S
ICMA Principles · SEBI BRSR · ISSB
F O R M A T
Lecture + Worked Problems
01

B E F O R E W E B E G I N
Labelled sustainable bonds have passed US$6.8 trillion.
Yet two ESG raters agree on a company’s score barely half the 
time.
Money is flowing toward sustainability faster than the measurement behind it is maturing. Today you learn both sides: 
how to raise green capital, and how to tell whether the “ESG” on the label is real.
SUSTAINABLE FINANCE 02

B Y T H E E N D O F T H I S L E C T U R E
You will be able to…
Classify
Tell green, social, sustainability-linked 
and transition instruments apart, and say 
what each promises.
Calculate
Work out a greenium, a carbon-adjusted 
valuation, and a portfolio’s carbon 
intensity (WACI).
Integrate
Show where ESG enters valuation, credit 
decisions and capital budgeting.
Evaluate
Spot greenwashing and rating 
divergence, and apply India’s SEBI and 
BRSR framework.
SUSTAINABLE FINANCE 03

T O D A Y ’ S J O U R N E Y
Finance: The Function That Prices Everything Else
After marketing, finance is the next function to integrate. It does two jobs for sustainability: it supplies capital to green projects, and it prices sustainability risk into 
every decision the other functions make.
01
Accessing Green Finance
The instruments, the rules, and how a 
company or government actually raises 
green money.
02
Integrating ESG into 
Decisions
Where ESG enters valuation, credit, and 
investment strategy, and why ratings 
disagree.
03
Measuring & Disclosing
BRSR, ISSB, and the metrics (WACI) that 
make financial claims checkable.
04
Integrity & Limits
Greenwashing in finance, the DWS case, 
and what the evidence does and does 
not show.
SUSTAINABLE FINANCE 04

S E C T I O N 1 O F 4
Accessing Green Finance
Capital is the raw material of every sustainability project. Here is where it comes from.
05

S E C T I O N 1 · D E F I N I T I O N
What Is Sustainable Finance?
Two directions of travel, often confused.
Financing Sustainability Directing capital to projects and companies that deliver environmental or social benefit: solar parks, electric rail, 
efficient buildings, affordable housing.
Making Finance Sustainable Taking environmental, social and governance (ESG) factors into every financial decision (lending, investing, 
valuing, insuring) because they change risk and return.
Two Lenses on Materiality Financial materiality asks how sustainability affects the company’s value. Double materiality adds how the 
company affects people and the planet. ISSB standards focus on the first; EU rules use the second.
SUSTAINABLE FINANCE 06

S E C T I O N 1 · T H E I N S T R U M E N T S
A Map of Sustainable Debt Instruments
Most labelled sustainable finance is debt. What differs is what the label actually promises.
Green Bonds
Proceeds are earmarked for eligible green projects. Repayment 
is the issuer’s ordinary obligation.
Social & Sustainability Bonds
Proceeds fund social projects (social bonds) or a mix of green 
and social projects (sustainability bonds).
Sustainability-Linked Bonds
Money can be used for anything, but the cost of the bond 
changes if the issuer misses a stated sustainability target.
Green Loans & SLLs
The bank-loan versions: use-of-proceeds green loans, and 
sustainability-linked loans whose margin moves with KPIs.
Transition Finance
Funding for high-emitting sectors to decarbonise credibly, such 
as steel, cement, and power. Controversial, and only as credible 
as the transition plan.
Blended Finance
Public or philanthropic money absorbs part of the risk to attract 
private capital into projects that would not otherwise be 
bankable.
SUSTAINABLE FINANCE 07

S E C T I O N 1 · T W O D E S I G N S
Use-of-Proceeds vs. KPI-Linked: What Is Actually Promised?
Green Bond (Use of Proceeds) Sustainability-Linked Bond (KPI)
What the money is for: specific, eligible green projects. What the money is for: general corporate purposes. Nothing is ring-fenced.
What is promised: proceeds are tracked and reported against the projects. What is promised: the issuer will hit a company-level target (the SPT) by a date.
Pricing consequence: usually none after issue; the label can bring a small 
pricing benefit (“greenium”).
Pricing consequence: the coupon steps up (typically 25 bp) if the target is 
missed.
Main integrity risk: projects that are not truly green, or proceeds that are not 
tracked.
Main integrity risk: targets that are easy to meet, or a step-up too small to 
matter.
SUSTAINABLE FINANCE 08

S E C T I O N 1 · T H E M A R K E T S T A N D A R D
The Four Core Components of the ICMA Green Bond 
Principles
Voluntary process guidelines, updated June 2025, that the market treats as the de facto standard.
1. Use of Proceeds
Proceeds go to eligible green projects 
with clear environmental benefits, 
described in the bond’s legal 
documentation.

◆ INTERACTIVE C A S E S T U D Y
Putting Money Where the Targets Are: Enel’s First SLB
Enel, September 2019: the first sustainability-linked bond
The Italian utility issued a US$1.5 billion five-year bond whose coupon depends on a company-wide KPI: raising renewable capacity to at least 55% of total installed 
capacity by the end of 2021, up from about 46% in mid-2019.
The Mechanism
If the target is missed, the coupon steps up by 25 basis points. The money itself is not ring￾fenced for any particular project.
The Market Response
Enel said the deal priced roughly 10 bp inside where a conventional bond would have 
priced, according to a law-firm case note. Demand was strong, and the structure was 
widely copied.
The Standard That Followed
ICMA published the Sustainability-Linked Bond Principles in June 2020: material KPIs, 
ambitious and benchmarked targets, a defined financial consequence, annual reporting, 
and independent verification.
The Criticism
Critics ask whether a 25 bp step-up is large enough to change behaviour, and whether 
targets are ambitious or merely continue existing trends. Both are questions an investor 
must test.

Three Channels Through Which ESG Reaches Value
A finance team does not need a separate “ESG model”. It needs ESG to show up in the models it already has.
Cash Flows Carbon costs, energy savings, regulatory fines, lost customers, and new green revenues change forecast 
revenues and costs directly.
Discount Rate Poor governance or high transition risk raises the return investors demand, lowering present value (as in the

A Carbon-Adjusted Valuation
G I V E N
Company EBITDA: ₹1,000 crore; valued at 8× EBITDA (EV = ₹8,000 crore)
Scope 1+2 emissions: 1,000,000 tCO₂e per year
Internal (shadow) carbon price used in analysis: ₹2,000 per tCO₂e
F O R M U L A
Carbon Cost = Emissions × Carbon Price
Adjusted EV = Multiple × (EBITDA − Carbon Cost)
S T E P - BY - S T E P C A L C U L A T I O N
1 Carbon cost: 1,000,000 t × ₹2,000/t = ₹2,000,000,000 = ₹200 crore
2 Adjusted EBITDA: ₹1,000 crore − ₹200 crore = ₹800 crore
3 Adjusted EV: 8 × ₹800 crore = ₹6,400 crore (down from ₹8,000 crore)
4 Change in value: ₹1,600 crore, or 20% lower
−20% Value A shadow carbon price turns an invisible risk into a number the investment committee can debate. (Illustrative: assumes no cost pass￾through and no abatement.)

Transition Risk Loans to emitters can lose value if carbon prices, regulation, or demand shifts reduce future cash flows (the

customers’ cash flows.
Project Finance: The Equator Principles Launched in 2003 and based on the IFC Performance Standards, they commit adopting banks to assess and 
manage environmental and social risk in project loans.

lower-risk clients.

Financed Emissions: Scope 3 Category 15 in Practice

S E C T I O N 3 · W O R K E D E X A M P L E
Weighted Average Carbon Intensity (WACI) of a Portfolio
G I V E N
Company A: 50% of portfolio; 100 tCO₂e per ₹ crore of revenue
Company B: 30% of portfolio; 400 tCO₂e per ₹ crore of revenue
Company C: 20% of portfolio; 50 tCO₂e per ₹ crore of revenue
F O R M U L A
WACI = Σ [ Portfolio Weight × (Scope 1+2 Emissions ÷ Revenue) ]
S T E P - BY - S T E P C A L C U L A T I O N
1 A: 0.50 × 100 = 50; B: 0.30 × 400 = 120; C: 0.20 × 50 = 10
2 WACI = 50 + 120 + 10 = 180 tCO₂e per ₹ crore of revenue
3 Rebalance: move 10 percentage points from B to A (A 60%, B 20%, C 20%)
4 New WACI = 0.60 × 100 + 0.20 × 400 + 0.20 × 50 = 60 + 80 + 10 = 150
180 → 150 (−17%) Shifting weight away from the most carbon-intensive holding cuts the metric. Caveat: intensity can fall just because revenue rises, so 
pair it with absolute emissions and real engagement.

Does ESG Pay? An Honest Reading
The strongest claims on both sides go beyond what the research supports.
Mixed, Not Magic Studies find ESG factors often act as risk indicators, but results vary by period, region, and method. “ESG always 
outperforms” is not established.
The Rater Problem Again Because ratings diverge, a result built on one provider’s ratings might not replicate with another’s (Berg et al., 
2022). Conclusions are only as good as the data behind them.
Small Price Benefits The sovereign greenium in India was about 6 bp. Green labels help diversify investors but are not a large cost 
saving.
A Contested Label In some markets “ESG” has become politically contested, and firms now talk more about risk, resilience, and 
transition. The underlying analysis (carbon cost, physical risk, governance) remains standard finance.

S E C T I O N 4 · A C H E C K L I S T
Five Checks for Credible Sustainable Finance
Before you buy, lend, issue, or recommend, ask whether the label survives these tests.
1. Is the Use Defined? Eligible projects or KPIs are specific, relevant to the issuer’s real footprint, and written down.
2. Is It Reviewed? An independent party has checked the framework or targets (Second Party Opinion, assurance).
3. Is the Target Ambitious? Targets go beyond business-as-usual trends and can be benchmarked against peers or science.
4. Is Reporting Verified? Allocation and impact are reported at least annually, with figures that auditors can test.
5. Is There a Consequence? Missing a target changes price or terms in a way that matters, such as a meaningful step-up.

S E C T I O N 1 · H O W C O S T S F A L L
Learning Curves: Why Deployment Is Itself Innovation
The pattern behind the solar and battery numbers.
Wright’s Law Unit cost falls by a roughly constant percentage each time cumulative production doubles. T.P. Wright first 
described it for aircraft manufacturing in 1936.
Why It Happens Scale economies, learning by doing, design simplification, supply-chain standardisation, and R&D that rides 
along with volume.
The Policy Lesson Volume drives cost, so demand-pull (auctions, mandates, public procurement) is innovation policy, not only 
subsidy.
The Caveat Learning rates are estimated from data, differ by technology, and are not guaranteed. Technologies limited by 
materials or physics may flatten.

S E C T I O N 1 · W O R K E D E X A M P L E
A Learning Curve: Five Doublings of Production
G I V E N
Initial unit cost: ₹100
Learning rate: 20% cost reduction per doubling of cumulative production 
(illustrative)
Cumulative production doubles five times
F O R M U L A
Cost after n doublings = C₀ × (1 − learning rate)ⁿ
S T E P - BY - S T E P C A L C U L A T I O N
1 Learning factor per doubling: 1 − 0.20 = 0.80
2 After five doublings: ₹100 × 0.80⁵ = ₹100 × 0.32768 ≈ ₹32.8
3 Cumulative volume needed: 2⁵ = 32 times the starting volume
4 Doublings to halve the cost: ln(0.5) ÷ ln(0.8) ≈ 3.1
−67% Cost A cost cut of two-thirds needs a 32-fold rise in cumulative volume. That is why early demand matters so much. (The 20% rate is 
illustrative; real rates must be measured.)

S E C T I O N 2 · T H E L A D D E R
Technology Readiness Levels (TRL): Nine Rungs from Idea to 
Market
Developed at NASA and now used by many funders, including the EU’s Horizon programmes, to say how mature a technology is.
TRL 1–3 · Research Basic principles observed, concept formulated, and experimental proof of concept in a laboratory.
TRL 4–6 · Development Validated in the lab (4), validated in a relevant environment (5), and a prototype demonstrated in a relevant environment (6).
TRL 7–9 · Deployment Prototype in an operational environment (7), system complete and qualified (8), and proven in real operation (9).
The Valley of Death Roughly TRL 5–8: costs jump, research grants stop, and commercial investors do not yet see proven returns.

S E C T I O N 2 · T H E F U N D I N G G A P
Why the Valley of Death Exists
The same gap appears in solar, batteries, hydrogen, and carbon capture.
Technology Risk and Market Risk Together A first-of-a-kind plant must prove that it works and that customers will pay. Investors can price one of those 
risks, not easily both.
Capital Intensity Moving from a ₹1 crore lab to a ₹200 crore demonstration plant multiplies the cheque while the evidence is still 
thin.
Who Bridges It Grants and demonstration funds, public procurement and offtake guarantees, development banks, and blended 
finance (see our sustainable finance lecture).

S E C T I O N 2 · W O R K E D E X A M P L E
The Innovation Funnel: Why Most Money Is Spent at the Last Gate
G I V E N
Stage A (lab to prototype): ₹1 crore each; 50% succeed. Stage B (prototype to 
demo): ₹20 crore each; 40% succeed
Stage C (demo to first commercial plant): ₹200 crore each; 70% succeed
Start with a portfolio of 100 technologies (illustrative figures)
F O R M U L A
Survivors = Start × p(A) × p(B) × p(C)
Spend = Σ (technologies entering stage × cost per stage)
S T E P - BY - S T E P C A L C U L A T I O N
1 Survivors: 100 × 0.5 × 0.4 × 0.7 = 14 technologies (14%)
2 Spend: A = 100 × ₹1 = ₹100 crore; B = 50 × ₹20 = ₹1,000 crore; C = 20 × ₹200 = ₹4,000 crore; total ₹5,100 crore
3 Cost per commercial success: ₹5,100 crore ÷ 14 ≈ ₹364 crore
4 Share of all spending at the last gate: ₹4,000 ÷ ₹5,100 ≈ 78%
78% at Gate C Most money is spent where risk is still high and revenue not yet proven, which is why public capital and offtake commitments are
decisive. Portfolio thinking matters: expect most to fail.

◆ INTERACTIVE C A S E S T U D Y
A Mission to Cross the Valley: India’s National Green Hydrogen Mission
National Green Hydrogen Mission (NGHM): approved by the Union Cabinet on 4 January 2023
The Mission allocates ₹19,744 crore to build 5 million tonnes a year of green hydrogen capacity by 2030, with about 125 GW of new renewable capacity. ₹17,490 crore 
goes to the SIGHT incentive programme; the rest to pilots, R&D, and other components.
Supply-Push and Demand-Pull
SIGHT pays incentives for domestic electrolyser manufacturing and for green hydrogen 
production, while green ammonia purchase agreements anchor demand at fertiliser plants.
Awards So Far
By August 2026: 3,000 MW a year of electrolyser manufacturing awarded to 15 companies; 
756,100 tonnes a year of hydrogen production capacity awarded; 670,000 tonnes a year of 
green ammonia contracted with 11 fertiliser units.
The Honest Gap
As of 6 August 2026 only ₹292 crore (about 1.5% of the outlay) had been spent, and 
awarded production capacity is about 15% of the 5 million tonne target.
The Lesson
Awards are not operating plants. Cost parity depends on electrolyser and renewable-power 
cost curves, and on demand that actually arrives.

◆ INTERACTIVE C A S E S T U D Y
AI as an Accelerator at the Front of the Pipeline: GNoME
Google DeepMind’s GNoME: Graph Networks for Materials Exploration (Nature, November 2023)
A graph neural network trained with active learning predicted the stability of inorganic crystals and identified about 2.2 million candidate structures, of which roughly 
380,000 are predicted most stable: a pre-filtered list for battery, solar and other clean-technology research.
The Scale
The Nature paper reports 381,000 newly discovered stable materials, almost an order of 
magnitude more than previous work, with predictions added to the open Materials Project 
database.
Validation So Far
736 of the structures have been independently made in laboratories worldwide, and an AI￾guided autonomous lab at Berkeley synthesised 41 new materials in a companion study.
Prediction Is Not Product
Predicting stability is not synthesising a material, nor showing that it is useful, affordable, 
and manufacturable. Those steps sit at TRL 3–7 and cost most.
Treat With Care
Published critiques question how many of the “new” materials are truly novel and useful. 
Read the counts as candidates, not as discoveries.
